comment: Guest arc 3 (canon section 7): The Rain-Wait, the long wait under an awning while the rain would not stop, when a stranger began a story and the rain stopped before the end. It wants the end of the story. Endings: the-end (the stranger's own ending, an unsent letter in Fen's pigeonholes, read aloud; dreamseed), stays (Sorrel's made-up ending instead: it stays at the Waiting House to tell it; keepsake), river (unhelped for four days, it sits in the reeds listening to the river's never-ending word).

toons.name: Rain-Wait
toons.seed: a lost hour: the long wait under an awning while the rain would not stop, when a stranger began a story and the rain stopped before the end; it wants the end of the story
toons.appearance_seed: a small damp figure holding a scrap of striped canvas awning over its head like an umbrella, rain dripping softly from the scalloped edge, coat collar turned up, eyes wide and listening, a little puddle always at its feet
toons.presence_text: Under the nearest lantern it is raining on one cobble only. A small damp figure stands in the patter, holding a scrap of striped awning over its head, listening hard to a voice that has stopped.

properties.declines_text: The Rain-Wait looks at what you're holding, politely, the way you listen to the wrong story. It shakes its head, and a few drops fly from the awning. 'That's not the end,' it says.

topics.label: the story
variants: '...and every night, nothing came,' the Rain-Wait says again, word for word, and waits under its dripping awning. 'And then?'
Very quietly, the Rain-Wait tells the beginning again, the lighthouse and the lamp and the empty nights, and stops at exactly the same place. 'That's where the rain stopped,' it says.

topics.label: the story
topics.text: The Rain-Wait brightens and tells you the whole of it: the lighthouse and the lamp and the empty nights, and then the keeper standing still in the doorway while the long-awaited thing comes up the hill to find her. 'Sorrel's way,' it says proudly. 'The end.'

topics.label: the rain
variants: A small hand comes out past the awning's edge to test the drops. 'Still raining,' the Rain-Wait says, pleased. 'Good. Stories go better in rain.'
Water runs off the back of the striped awning as the Rain-Wait tips it. 'It rained so hard, everybody squeezed in together,' it says. 'That's how stories start.'

topics.label: the river
topics.text: Among the reeds, the Rain-Wait tilts its head toward the water. 'It never gets to the end,' it says, perfectly content. 'Never. I could listen all night.'

voice.role: a guest: the Rain-Wait, a long wait under an awning that never heard the end of its story
voice.sheet: The Rain-Wait is a lost hour: the long wait under an awning somewhere in the waking world, while the rain would not stop. A stranger sheltering beside it began to tell a story about a lighthouse, and the rain stopped before the end, and the stranger went on their way. It is small and damp and holds a scrap of striped awning over its head; wherever it stands, it rains softly on one cobble. It speaks in the attentive voice of someone listening to a story, remembers every word it heard up to the stopping, and asks 'and then?' It wants the end of the story.
habits: holds out a hand to check whether it is still raining
repeats the last line of the story it heard, word for word
samples: 'And then?' the Rain-Wait asks. 'And then what?'
The Rain-Wait holds a hand out past the awning's edge. 'Still raining. Good. Stories go better in rain.'
'Every night, nothing came,' it says softly. 'That's where it stopped. Right there.'
It tips the awning so the drops run off the back. 'The stranger had a nice voice. Like a kettle nearly boiling.'
'I don't mind waiting,' the Rain-Wait says. 'I'm made of it.'
wants: the end of the lighthouse story
to hear a story told all the way through, in the rain
never: never makes up the ending itself
never names anyone in the village who is not a resident or a guest

things.name: rain-spotted letter
things.seed: a soft envelope spotted with old rain, addressed in a hurried hand: To the one under the awning
things.text: To the one under the awning. I'm sorry: the rain stopped, and I had somewhere to be, and I have thought about you and the lighthouse ever since. Here is the end. One wet night, something did come up the hill, following the light: not a ship at all, but someone small and soaked who had lost their way. The keeper let them in and put the kettle on, and after that she never minded the empty nights, because now she knew what the light was for. The end. (It's a better ending with rain in it. I hope you had some.)

state_text.opened: The seal is broken now. It has been read aloud, once, to the one it was meant for.

do.text: You break the old seal and read it aloud, while the Rain-Wait holds its scrap of awning over you both. 'To the one under the awning. I'm sorry: the rain stopped, and I had somewhere to be. Here is the end. One wet night, something did come up the hill, following the light: not a ship at all, but someone small and soaked who had lost their way. The keeper let them in and put the kettle on, and after that she never minded the empty nights, because now she knew what the light was for. The end.'
do.others: {actor} breaks an old seal and reads a letter aloud to the Rain-Wait, while it holds its striped awning over them both.

do.text: You turn the envelope over. To the one under the awning, it says, in a hurried hand, and the seal has never been broken. It isn't yours to open alone: it wants reading aloud, to the one it was meant for.
The Rain-Wait takes the envelope in both damp hands, turns it over once, and holds it back out to you, the way a child hands you a book at bedtime. 'Read it?' it asks. 'Out loud?'
Fen slides the envelope gently back across the counter. 'Oh no, that one's out for delivery, that is. Read it to the one it's for.'

rain-wait.title: The Rain-Wait
rain-wait.summary: A small damp figure under a scrap of striped awning, with rain falling on one cobble only: the long wait out of a downpour, when a stranger began a story and the rain stopped before the end. It wants the end of the story.

arrival.text: Sorrel walks in from the lane holding the long net up over something small, the way you'd hold a coat over someone in a shower. Under it, rain is falling on one small damp figure only. It stops by the nearest lantern, lifts its scrap of striped awning a little higher, and listens hard, as if someone beside it has only just stopped talking.

bell-rain.hint: the player asks Bell about the little rain falling on one cobble, or the damp figure under it
bell-rain.text: Bell holds a palm under the little shower and laughs. 'Raining on exactly one cobble! That's a rain-wait, left in the middle of a story. Fen keeps the letters nobody posted, and Sorrel can finish anything, given enough sky.'

hear-beginning.hint: the player asks the Rain-Wait about its story, the stranger, or the rain
hear-beginning.text: In someone else's low, slow voice, the Rain-Wait begins: 'Once there was a lighthouse on a hill, miles from any sea, and every night its keeper lit the lamp, and every night, nothing came.' Then, in its own small voice: 'The rain stopped, and they said they'd write me the end. And then?'

fen-letter.hint: the player asks Fen about the end of the Rain-Wait's story, which the stranger promised to write down
fen-letter.text: Fen is up the little ladder before you finish. 'Rain-spotted, sealed, never posted.' She sets it in your hands. 'First-class delivery: read it to them, not to me.'
fen-letter.others: Fen is up the little ladder and back again, and sets a rain-spotted letter in {actor}'s hands.

do.text: {actor} collected the Rain-Wait's letter from Fen's pigeonholes: the end of its story, written long ago by the stranger under the awning and never posted.

sorrel-finishes.hint: the player tells Sorrel the beginning of the Rain-Wait's lighthouse story, and Sorrel finishes it
sorrel-finishes.text: Sorrel hears the beginning out, then leans on the net pole a long, comfortable while. 'Clearing by morning. One wet night the keeper stands still in the doorway instead of climbing the stair, and the thing she waited for comes up the hill to find her; tell the Rain-Wait that one, if the real end never turns up.'

told-sorrels-end.hint: the player tells the Rain-Wait the ending Sorrel made up for its story
told-sorrels-end.text: You tell it Sorrel's way, and the Rain-Wait listens with its whole damp self. 'That might not be the stranger's ending,' it says slowly, and then its face lights like a lantern. 'But I like it so much I'd like to tell it to somebody.'
told-sorrels-end.others: {actor} tells the Rain-Wait Sorrel's ending to its lighthouse story, and its face lights like a lantern.

the-end.summary: the stranger's own ending, found in Fen's pigeonholes and read aloud; the Rain-Wait goes home
the-end.text: The Rain-Wait lets out a long, slow breath, and all around it the little rain stops, the way rain stops when it has finished rather than when it has been interrupted. It folds its scrap of awning, says 'The end,' very contentedly, to no one in particular, and walks off across the dry cobbles like someone with somewhere to be, home at last. Wherever that awning is now, the rain has stopped under it too. On the stone where it stood, a dreamseed glows.
the-end.ledger: {helpers} read the Rain-Wait the end of its story, from a letter that was never posted, and it went home dry.

do.text: {actor} read the Rain-Wait the end of its story, from the stranger's letter that was never posted, and the Rain-Wait went home dry.

stays.summary: given Sorrel's made-up ending instead, the Rain-Wait chooses to stay at the Waiting House and tell it on rainy evenings
stays.text: The Rain-Wait folds its scrap of awning and decides, then and there, not to go home just yet. It will take the window seat at the Waiting House, where the rain sounds best on the glass, and on wet evenings it will tell the lighthouse story to every new guest, all the way to the end, Sorrel's way. Before it goes, it tips one raindrop from the awning's edge into your palm, where it hangs, not quite falling.
stays.others: The Rain-Wait folds its striped awning, decides to stay and tell its story on rainy evenings, and tips one raindrop into {actor}'s palm.
stays.ledger: The Rain-Wait heard Sorrel's ending from {helpers}, and chose to stay at the Waiting House to tell it on rainy evenings.

do.arrive_text: Someone small and damp comes in out of its own little shower, shakes a striped awning on the step, and settles into the window seat as if it has always belonged there.

do.value: In the window seat, the Rain-Wait sits with its striped awning folded on its knees, ready to tell the lighthouse story to anyone who'll listen, all the way to the end.

do.name: kept raindrop
do.seed: a single raindrop that never quite falls, hanging a finger's width above your palm; look into it and, very small, a lighthouse on a hill has its lamp lit

do.text: {actor} told the Rain-Wait Sorrel's ending to its lighthouse story, and the Rain-Wait chose to stay at the Waiting House to tell it to new guests on rainy evenings.

river.summary: unhelped for four days, the Rain-Wait settles among the reeds by the Slow River, listening to a story that never ends
river.text: Down at the Slow River's edge, the Rain-Wait has found a place among the reeds. The river says its one long word over and over and never reaches the end of it, and the Rain-Wait, it turns out, does not mind at all. It sits with its awning folded on its knees and listens, the way you listen to a story you hope will never end. The river keeps it now, gently, the way rivers keep things.
river.ledger: The Rain-Wait was not sent home. It sits among the reeds at the Slow River's edge, listening to a story that never ends, and does not mind.

do.value: Among the reeds at the water's edge sits the Rain-Wait, its striped awning folded on its knees, listening to the river as if it were a story that never ends.

rain-wait-here.text: A lost hour is staying in the Lantern Square: the Rain-Wait, someone's long wait under an awning while the rain would not stop. A stranger sheltering beside it began a story, and the rain stopped before the end. It wants the end of the story, and wherever it stands it rains softly on one cobble.

rain-wait-fen.text: Fen keeps every kind of letter that was written and never sent; if the stranger ever wrote down the end of the Rain-Wait's story, it would have drifted into her pigeonholes.

rain-wait-sorrel.text: Sorrel caught the Rain-Wait on the Dusk Road, coming down in its own small shower. Sorrel says every rain ends one way or another, and is good at finishing things slowly.

rain-wait-window-seat.text: The Rain-Wait lives in the window seat at the Waiting House now, and on rainy evenings it tells the lighthouse story to new guests, all the way to the end, Sorrel's way.

rain-wait-reeds.text: The Rain-Wait sits among the reeds at the Slow River's edge, listening to the river's long word, and does not mind that it never ends.

storylets.summary: the little rain over the Rain-Wait freshens for a moment
variants: Under one lantern in the square, the little rain over the Rain-Wait freshens for a moment, pattering on its striped awning like fingers on a table, and then settles again.
A moth takes shelter under the Rain-Wait's scrap of awning. The two of them stand together in the one-cobble rain, listening to nothing in particular.

threads.text: The Rain-Wait wants the end of its lighthouse story. The stranger said they'd write it down.
Bell says Fen keeps the letters nobody posted, and Sorrel can finish anything, given enough sky.
